newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-Dlr rally vs yen seen running off track.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Dlr rally vs yen seen running off track.

text.p: Concern about an expanding Japanese trade surplus with the United States could soon derail a rally that powered the dollar to its highest level in 56 months against the yen, said analysts in a Reuters poll.

Since soaring to 127.16 yen on April 10, the dollar has hovered just below its peak. But this modest pullback will likely turn into a steady decline that deepens throughout the remainder of this year and the next, according to the latest Reuters quarterly U.S. economic survey.
"The main rationale for that is what is going to be the rapidly accumulating Japanese trade surplus," said Gail Fosler, senior vice president and chief economist of the Conference Board.
As the Japanese trade surplus with the United States increases, political tension between the two countries is going to drive down the dollar, said Fosler.
A Reuters poll of 19 analysts, on average, projected the dollar will fetch 126.25 yen at the end of the second quarter and slide to 121.72 yen by the close of the fourth.
This retreat is seen continuing in 1998, with the greenback declining to 118.08 yen by the end of the first quarter and 113.90 by the close of the final quarter.
Japan's trade surplus with the United States swelled in January, February and March.
This has already prompted some Clinton Administration officials to warn the Japanese government against trying to export its way out of economic difficulties.
Besides the potential for escalating trade friction between Japan and the United States, some analysts expected the dollar rally to run out of steam simply because it has already lasted too long.
Since tumbling to a post World War II low of 79.75 yen on April 19, 1995, the dollar has gained about 59 percent against the yen.
"The principle thing is I think it (the rally) has been somewhat overdone," said David Blitzer, a vice president and chief economist at Standard & Poor's.
Blitzer doubted that the prospect for higher U.S. interest rates will drive the dollar much higher.
